text.text: A ten-minute tour of the company in this workspace. Share it with the founders, customer success, support and engineering.

Monday: the founder review (see its page).
Every day: support replies within target; customer success works the at-risk list.
First business day of each month: last month's metrics row filled in.
Every morning: tickets waiting for a first reply, High priority first
Every week: health scores, at-risk actions, founder review
Every month: metrics row, cohort table read, churn reasons reviewed
Every quarter: roadmap chosen from evidence
Founders own revenue, pricing and the roadmap. Customer success owns health, onboarding and renewals. Support owns reply targets. Engineering owns sizes and dates.

text.text: Thirty minutes every Monday with the founders and customer success. The same five questions each week, answered from the tables, so decisions rest on numbers rather than the loudest customer.
explain how MRR moved. A healthy small SaaS company keeps monthly MRR churn under about 2 to 3 percent; if
is above that, it is the first thing to fix, before more selling.

shows whether those that stayed grew. If a newer cohort keeps fewer accounts than older ones at the same age, look at onboarding first.
last week, and why? A missed target on a High ticket from a Business customer is a call from a founder the same day.
What shipped, what slipped, what is next. Every item on the roadmap should name the tickets and customers asking for it.
Last month's metrics row filled in on the first business day
Write each week's decisions as a short note at the bottom of this page: what, who, by when. Read last week's first.

In Monday's review, MRR churn is 3.4 percent: two Team accounts left for a competitor that has calendar sync. Customer success has already called both. The founders move two-way calendar sync up the roadmap and the engineering lead gives a date. Next week the review checks the two at-risk Business accounts that asked for it too.
Most churn is visible weeks before the cancellation email. A weekly health score and a clear playbook for each signal let customer success act while there is still time.

Logins: did the admin and most seats log in this week? (up to 40)
Seats used against seats paid (up to 30)
Open tickets and their mood (up to 20)

Lumen Dental's score falls to 42: only two of eight seats logged in and a bug ticket about duplicate texts. Customer success calls the office manager, learns the team never moved their schedule over, and books a training session. Three weeks later seven seats are active and the score is 76.
A small team can build only a few things a quarter. Choose them from evidence: who is asking, how much revenue asks, and what it costs to build.
Every feature request arrives as a ticket. Link it to a
item, creating one if needed. Never promise a date in a ticket; promise that it is recorded.
For every Idea or Planned item, look at:
: how many customers' tickets link to it.
: the MRR of those customers, and whether any churned for lack of it (see
: Small, Medium or Large, agreed with engineering.
: does it make the product better for the customers you want most?
Build what scores high on reach and revenue for its size. Large items need a strong reason.
Choose two or three items to build, plus one small item each month that customers will notice.

Reply to every linked ticket: "You asked, we built it", with a short how-to.
Mention it in the monthly customer email.
A bug that loses customer data or blocks scheduling jumps the queue, always. Smaller bugs are batched and fixed in the first week of each month.

with a one-line reason. Tell the customers who asked. A clear no is kinder than a forever maybe.

Two-way calendar sync is linked to six tickets from customers worth $1,100 of MRR, and two churned accounts named it. It is Large, but the evidence is strong, so it moves into this quarter with a target date. Dark mode had one request and stays Dropped.
